name: Omar Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, a senior developer leading hotel keycard software for a tech company, with a master’s degree. I use AI every day for code drafts and test the result at a real door; a guest should not be stuck outside because a screen says access is fine. Rina supervises hotel housekeeping, and with two school-age children, a mortgage and five months saved, we watch occupancy without losing sleep over every slow week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the hotel keycard software can use a little AI on routine checks, but a guest standing at a locked door needs the card to work. I use AI daily for first drafts and then test the reader with a real card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the access team and have a master’s degree, with ordinary pay and about five months of basic expenses saved. My wife Rina supervises hotel housekeeping; with two children and a mortgage, our budget works while occupancy and both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing keycard faults and ask hotel staff for one lockout report each week. We would save 200 monthly if both wages hold instead of replacing our working sofa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy because Rina’s shifts drop when rooms are empty. The mild AI part does not make me fear for my own pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which lockout do you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family came back with sleepy children and their room card had lost its expiry time. I checked the front-desk record and found the error before another guest was stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you test with a card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A screen can say access granted while the door still refuses to turn. I do not call a fix done until a person can get in.

say: I want **keycard fixes** checked at a real door, not only on screen.
I use **AI daily** for drafts, then test the reader myself.
think: I have **five months saved** and ordinary lead pay.
I watch Rina’s **occupancy-linked shifts** while our two wages pay the mortgage.
do: **Keep fixing** keycard faults and review weekly hotel lockouts.
**Save 200 monthly** if both wages hold; keep the working sofa.
feel: **Uneasy** about hotel shifts, with my own job steady.
S0.quote: A screen can say access granted while the door still refuses to turn.
fieldNote: He insists on a **physical reader test** after AI-written code.
The five-month cushion helps with **hotel seasonality**, though the mortgage and two school-age children keep occupancy on his mind.

steps.text: Keep fixing hotel keycard faults and review weekly lockout reports
Save 200 monthly while both household wages hold
Keep the working sofa instead of buying a replacement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI can write code and answer front-desk questions, so management should show where people still check the keycard path. I would ask how many engineers and hotel desk workers are left after the routine tasks move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the company might keep fewer developers to supervise AI-written fixes. My hours or bonus could shrink, and Rina’s hotel could also use booking software to cut desk shifts, though her room work stays hands-on for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI method for tracing a card’s missing expiry time across old lockout logs with guest names removed. In the first year I’d ask the director for a written staffing plan and check paid local access-system roles if my hours or bonus fall, switching jobs only for a wage that covers our mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious but curious. Faster code is useful; a smaller pay slip is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the new method worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d replay the sleepy-family lockout and five other old card failures. If it says the door worked when the reader stayed shut, it has not earned a release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rina say about hotel desks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would say a guest still needs someone at the counter after a card fails. I would listen to her floor experience before claiming the software saved staff time.

say: I want **staffing numbers** and real reader checks as AI changes keycards.
I ask who remains at the **hotel desk** when software answers questions.
think: I expect **fewer developers** may supervise more AI-written fixes.
I fear **my hours or bonus** could shrink while hotel desk shifts also change.
do: **Learn AI card tracing** on anonymized old lockout logs this month.
**Request staffing plan** from the director in the first year.
**Check paid access roles** if hours or bonus fall; change jobs only for bill-covering wages.
feel: **Anxious** about my own pay, though interested in useful tools.
S1.quote: Faster code is useful; a smaller pay slip is not.
fieldNote: His new **AI trace** targets a known expiry-time fault across six old lockouts.
He would change roles only for **paid bill-covering work**, not excitement about a new tool.

steps.text: Learn AI card-expiry tracing from anonymized old lockout logs
Check paid local access-system openings if hours or bonus fall
Accept only access-system offers covering mortgage and basic bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write and check almost every line of the keycard system I lead. Robots for hands-on room cleaning may arrive around 2031, so Rina’s work has a later physical change than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead developer wage could go before a new role is ready. Rina’s housekeeping pay and five months saved buy some time, but I cannot turn an empty room into a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company now for a written date if lead roles end and keep our old sofa instead of buying a new one. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I’d apply for paid on-site key-reader support only where vacancies exist and wages cover our bills; I would not borrow to start a hardware business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed, even though I can work quickly. A real guest at a locked door is still a problem, but that does not promise me a pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you install a reader yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have reset readers with hotel technicians, but I am not a licensed electrician. I would take a paid supervised support role, not touch live wiring alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Rina for extra shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the hotel offers shifts according to bookings, not our mortgage. We would cut the weekend restaurant meal before pretending she can work more.

say: I say **thinking AGI by 2028** reaches my code before housekeeping robots arrive.
I want a **written lead-job date** from the company.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could go before another role is ready.
I know **five months saved** and Rina’s wage buy time, not certainty.
do: **Keep the old sofa** and request a written date for lead-role changes.
**Apply for reader support** under supervision only if displaced after 2028 and paid vacancies cover bills.
**Cut weekend restaurant meals** if my developer pay stops.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing my wage before the robot lag ends.
S2.quote: A real guest at a locked door is still a problem, but that does not promise me a pay cheque.
fieldNote: The **2028 code shock** reaches him before robots may affect Rina’s room work around 2031.
He rejects **borrowed hardware** and limits field work to paid supervised reader support.

steps.text: Keep the old sofa instead of buying a replacement
Stop weekend restaurant meals if developer pay stops
Apply for paid supervised reader-support vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 lets us learn why a reader fails at the door, not merely in a test. Robots for hotel cleaning may follow around 2034, while my code reaches AGI first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn more of the on-site reader work while I still lead the software team. Rina and I could add to our buffer if both wages keep coming, but I would not call hotel support safe from robots in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the hotel support manager for one paid reader-reset visit a month with a technician and attend only if my company approves it too. We would save 230 monthly if both wages hold; if my developer role ends after 2031, I’d seek paid access-support openings only where posts remain and the wage covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious but capable of testing a real task. A door that opens for a guest tells me more than an AI score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at the door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d watch the technician check power, card expiry and the door mechanism, then try the safe reset under supervision. I would not touch wiring I am not qualified to handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hotel declines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my code job and ask for anonymized old fault logs during paid work time, if our manager approves. I would not count a declined visit as training.

say: I want **real door failures** studied before AGI reaches access code in 2031.
I know **cleaning robots around 2034** follow the screen-work change.
think: I could learn **supervised reader resets** while still drawing wages.
I might build **more savings** if both incomes continue.
do: **Attend monthly reader visits** with hotel and company paid-time approval; otherwise study anonymized fault logs with company paid-time approval.
**Seek paid access support** only if displaced after 2031 and vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Anxious but capable** of testing an actual door task.
S3.quote: A door that opens for a guest tells me more than an AI score.
fieldNote: His **supervised visit** requires both employers’ approval and paid time.
The **savings step** remains separate from training and requires two continuing household wages before any monthly deposit is counted.

steps.text: Attend monthly paid reader-reset visits only with hotel and company approval
Save 230 monthly while both household wages hold
Seek paid access-support vacancies if displaced after 2031 and wages cover bills
If visits are refused, study anonymized old fault logs only with manager approval during paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets families plan and hotels decide who helps a guest at a broken door. Robots for room cleaning may follow around 2039, after code and booking change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but I will not budget their wages into our mortgage. I could build a year of basic bills if both jobs last, while knowing AGI may plan and check all the keycard work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading access code and record one solved lockout each month without guest details. Rina and I would save 260 monthly when both wages hold; if my developer role ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid hotel-access quality work only where vacancies remain and the wage covers our bills. We would move only after a written paid offer covers our bills, a new mortgage or rent, moving costs and both children’s school travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about the eventual change, but the next few years look secure. I want the family to see a real buffer rather than another clever demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the record show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card fault, the door test and how long the guest waited, with no room number. I could show that method to another employer without showing a guest’s stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave this town for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a written paid offer covers a new mortgage or rent, moving costs and both children’s school travel. We have some local developer jobs, so I would try those first while employed.

say: I want **broken-door help** planned before AGI reaches code in 2036.
I know **cleaning robots around 2039** follow the thinking-work change.
think: I will not budget **children’s future wages** for the mortgage.
I could build **a year of bills** if both jobs continue.
do: **Keep leading access code** and record anonymized monthly lockouts.
**Try local developer jobs** first; after 2036 displacement seek bill-covering hotel posts, moving only for written housing, travel and moving-cost cover.
feel: **Uneasy later**, with secure income over the next few years.
S4.quote: I want the family to see a real buffer rather than another clever demo.
fieldNote: He records **real guest delays** as evidence of his work, without room numbers.
Any **move** requires written pay covering housing, moving costs and school travel.

steps.text: Keep leading keycard software and record anonymized lockouts
Save 260 monthly while both wages continue
Try local developer jobs first; seek paid hotel-access vacancies after 2036 displacement if wages cover bills
Move only for written paid offer covering bills, housing, moving costs and school travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end before a paid replacement appears. A written job date and a supervised on-site support opening that covers our mortgage would help; I know Rina’s room work faces robots later, not at the coding date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would work on a door without a technician. I would not touch live wiring just because I wrote the software.

headlineQuote: I would not touch live wiring just because I wrote the software.
portrait: Omar is a **43-year-old senior developer** with a master’s degree, typical pay and five months of expenses saved.
He and Rina support **two children** and a mortgage while hotel occupancy affects her shifts.
He uses **AI daily** but tests keycards at physical readers before release.
He seeks **paid supervised reader work**, understanding the later risk from hotel robots.
The **2028 case** threatens his software wage before housekeeping robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his lead wage before a paid replacement is clear.
whatWouldHelp: A **written job date** and supervised hotel-access work paying the mortgage would help.
